newsitem.title: UK: British TV chief pleads for fairer tax system.
newsitem.headline: British TV chief pleads for fairer tax system.

text.p: Britain's terrestrial broadcasters, facing heavy costs from investing in digital television, need a fairer taxation system, a leading TV chief said on Thursday.

Clive Hollick, chief executive of United News & Media, told parliament's National Heritage select committee that independent television companies will need to spend up to 200 million pounds ($324 million) to gear up for digital TV.

Cable operators are also moving into the digital world. Stephen Davidson, chairman of the Cable Communications Association, told the committee that operators intended to launch a national digital television service later in 1997.

BSkyB plans to launch digital satellite into the UK later this year offering some 200 channels. Digital terrestrial television (DTT), broadcast from land-based transmitters and showing over 30 channels, is set to begin by mid-1998.

Hollick said that the ITV commercial television companies would have to spend 10 million pounds annually to broadcast their programmes on DTT. He said that 100-200 million pounds of capital expenditure was needed for the switch to digital.
That investment will come on top of the 400 million pounds that commercial television companies currently pay to the Treasury each year, over and above corporation tax payments.

"That is a considerable financial burden on the industry at a time when it is investing in digital," Hollick said. "The taxation system needs looking at again and I would argue for a fairer system that spreads across all broadcasters."

United News & Media owns independent TV companies Meridian and Anglia -- which broadcast to the south of England and East Anglia respectively. It also holds stakes in Yorkshire Tyne Tees Television and HTV.
Hollick said the additional revenue from investing in digital was highly uncertain, at least in the short-term. "Digital could well lose money for three or four years."
Hollick, a Labour-supporting peer, argued the taxation system should be broadened to cover all broadcasters.
"Continuing the present regime will ultimately undermine the achievements of UK broadcasting over the past decades. It is time to change them," a United News statement said.
A number of politicians on the committee voiced concerns about a fall in the quality of television programming once hundreds of broadcasters started jostling for position.

Hollick said many of the new channels would offer niche services, a specialist cookery channel was one example he cited. But he said the main territorial firms would remain dedicated to high-quality programme making, as their licences demanded.
